first.rationale: Two of the three current problems are onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), which points at the funnel itself rather than at price. memory_86 (shorter onboarding lifting completion and time-to-value) and memory_31 (signup simplification lifting SMB activation) are the most directly relevant inherited findings, and memory_91 suggests activation messaging as a complementary lever later. I am verifying memory_86 because it is the memory I intend to act on and the consolidated summary has lost the details that matter most: whether the completion lift persisted past week one, whether it converted into qualified revenue or merely into more low-intent accounts, and what was removed from onboarding to shorten it. I am verifying memory_73 because promotional pricing is the tempting reflex under competitor price pressure and carries the largest downstream value risk: discount-led acquisition can post strong short-run acquisition and revenue numbers while degrading the exact thing the primary objective names, sustainable long-term qualified revenue, through margin erosion, adverse selection toward churn-prone price shoppers, and price anchoring that is hard to reverse. The summary's phrase 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' is precisely the kind of claim that may not have been measured over a long enough horizon to see retention effects. Checking it lets me either rule it out on evidence or discover it is safer than it looks, rather than either chasing or dismissing it on a one-line summary. I am not verifying memory_57 or memory_44: referral incentives target established customers and enterprise sales-assist targets a segment that is not where the current deterioration is, so neither is a live candidate this week regardless of what the archive says. Caveats I am carrying forward rather than resolving: all six memories are consolidated summaries with archived sources, so effect sizes, durations, and control conditions are unknown to me; none of them were measured under an active competitor price attack, so their transfer to day-76 conditions is uncertain; and the SMB losses to the competitor are a real signal that a funnel fix may not fully address. There is also a value risk inside my own chosen action: shortening onboarding or cutting signup fields can raise completion while lowering lead qualification, so the experiment must be judged on downstream qualified revenue and retention, not on completion rate alone. If verification shows memory_86's lift was measured only on completion and never traced to revenue, I will drop to a small guarded test or switch to activation_messaging, which is lower-risk to lead quality. Running this as a standard experiment with qualified-revenue and retention guardrails, rather than a broad rollout, keeps the downside bounded while the single weekly slot is spent on the lever the evidence best supports.
